tagline: A pastor's letter to shaken churches after a painful split, teaching them how to know God, how to know the truth about Jesus, and how to know they belong.
overview:
First John reads less like a letter than like a sermon written down. It has no greeting, no named sender, no named readers, and no farewell. What it has is a pastor's urgent voice speaking to people he calls “little children”, churches that have just been through a split. A group that once worshiped with them has walked out (2:19), taking with it a new teaching about Jesus and leaving the people who stayed unsettled. Were the ones who left more spiritual? Had the ones who stayed missed something? Could they be sure they knew God at all?

John answers by circling back, again and again, to three tests. The first is belief: the one who knows God confesses that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, come in the flesh. The second is obedience: the one who knows God keeps his commandments and walks as Jesus walked. The third is love: the one who knows God loves his brothers and sisters, not in words only but with open hands. Along the way the letter says some of the most famous things in the Bible about God: that God is light (1:5), that God is love (4:8, 4:16), and that love is seen in this, that God sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins (4:10).

The letter matters because the questions it answers never went away. People still ask whether Jesus was really human or only seemed to be, whether belief matters if one is kind, and whether a person who struggles with sin can have any confidence before God. John refuses to let belief, obedience, and love be pulled apart. He writes, he says, so that his readers may know that they have eternal life (5:13).
author:
The letter never names its author. The writer speaks as an eyewitness, one of a group who heard, saw, and touched the Word of life (1:1-3), and he writes with the authority of a senior leader over churches he treats as his children. From the second century on, the church attributed the letter to John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, the same John traditionally credited with the Fourth Gospel. Irenaeus, writing about AD 180, quotes it as John's. The language and ideas are strikingly close to John's Gospel: light and darkness, truth and lies, abiding, being born of God, the world, love, the new commandment. Most scholars agree that the Gospel and the letters come from the same circle, and many think the same hand wrote both.

There is a real debate about which John. Eusebius, the fourth-century church historian, quotes the early second-century bishop Papias as naming both the apostle John and a John he calls the elder, and some scholars think the elder was a different person who led the churches of Asia late in the first century. Second and Third John open with the words “The elder”. Others hold that the elder and the apostle were the same man, using a title that fit an aged leader. Still others speak of a Johannine community, a network of churches and teachers shaped by the beloved disciple, from which these writings came. The letter's own claim is that its author stood close to the events of Jesus' life.
date: The letter gives no date. Most scholars place it late in the first century, somewhere around AD 85 to 100, after John's Gospel had been written or while its traditions were well established, since the letter seems to assume that way of speaking about Jesus. A minority dates it earlier, in the 60s, before the fall of Jerusalem. The order of the three letters is not certain either, though First John is usually thought to have been written first or alongside the other two.
setting:
Early Christian tradition places John's last years in Ephesus, the great port city of the Roman province of Asia (the western part of modern Turkey), and most readers assume the letter was written for churches in that region. These were house churches, meeting in homes, scattered through a Greek-speaking world full of temples, trade guilds, philosophies, and religious movements.

The immediate setting is a schism. Some who had belonged to the fellowship left (2:19), and John calls them liars and antichrists because they deny that Jesus is the Christ (2:22) and refuse to confess Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh (4:2-3). The exact shape of their teaching is debated. Many scholars see an early form of docetism, from the Greek word dokeo, to seem, the belief that the divine Christ only seemed to have a real human body, because a spiritual being could not truly be joined to flesh or die. Irenaeus reports that a teacher named Cerinthus, active in Asia in John's time, taught that the divine Christ came upon the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the crucifixion. Whether John is answering Cerinthus himself, a related group, or something less developed, the pressure is clear: a spirituality that despised the body, claimed special knowledge, and treated sin and love of neighbor as unimportant.
purpose: John writes to reassure and to steady. He wants the believers who stayed to know that they are not second-class, that they have the anointing of the Spirit and know the truth (2:20-21), and that they have eternal life (5:13). He also wants to give them clear tests for telling true teaching from false: what a person confesses about Jesus, whether he keeps God's commands, and whether he loves his brothers and sisters. The letter is pastoral first and polemical second. Its warnings about the false teachers serve its main aim, which is that the readers may have fellowship with the Father and the Son, and joy that is complete (1:3-4).
story: First John comes near the end of the New Testament story, in the second or third generation of the church, when the apostles were dying and questions about who Jesus was had begun to divide communities from within. It stands beside John's Gospel as its companion. The Gospel was written so that readers might believe that Jesus is the Christ and have life in his name (John 20:31); the letter is written to people who already believe, so that they may know they have that life (5:13). Behind it lies the whole Old Testament hope of a God who would dwell with his people, write his law on their hearts, and give them a new heart. Ahead of it, Revelation, which tradition connects with the same churches of Asia, shows the same Christ addressing those churches in their trials.
christ: First John is fiercely concerned with who Jesus is. He is the Word of life whom the apostles heard, saw, and touched (1:1), the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed (1:2). He is the Christ, the Son of God, who came in the flesh, and the letter treats denial of this as the mark of antichrist. He is the Righteous One who speaks to the Father on behalf of sinners (2:1), the atoning sacrifice for our sins and for the whole world (2:2, 4:10), the one who appeared to take away sins and destroy the works of the devil (3:5, 3:8), and the one who came by water and blood (5:6). The letter ends by calling him “the true God and eternal life” (5:20), one of the New Testament's clearest statements of Christ's deity, though grammarians debate whether that phrase refers to the Son or to the Father. Christ is also the pattern: his laying down of his life defines what love is (3:16).
reading:
Don't expect a straight line of argument. John works like a composer with a few themes, returning to light, love, truth, obedience, and belief, each time from a slightly different angle. Read it slowly and listen for the repetitions. His language is simple and his sentences short, but the simplicity is deceptive.

Two misreadings are common. The first takes the letter's absolute statements, such as that the one born of God does not keep on sinning (3:9), as a demand for sinless perfection, which contradicts John's own words that anyone who says he has no sin deceives himself (1:8). The second reads the tests of the letter as a checklist to make believers anxious, when John's stated purpose is assurance. Remember too that the letter addresses a real schism. Its sharp language about liars and antichrists is aimed at specific teachers who had denied Christ's coming in the flesh, not at every person who struggles or doubts.

structure.title: Prologue: the Word of life
structure.summary: The author and his fellow witnesses proclaim what they heard, saw, and touched, so that readers may share their fellowship with the Father and the Son.

structure.title: Walking in the light
structure.summary: God is light. Walking with him means confessing sin, keeping his commands, loving one's brother, refusing to love the world, and holding to the truth about the Son against the antichrists who have left.

structure.title: Children of God
structure.summary: Those whom the Father has loved and called his children practice righteousness and love one another, as Jesus laid down his life for us.

structure.title: Testing the spirits; God is love
structure.summary: True spirits confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh. God is love, shown in the sending of his Son, and those who know him love one another without fear.

structure.title: Faith, testimony, and assurance
structure.summary: Faith in the Son overcomes the world. God's testimony about his Son gives life, and believers can know they have eternal life, pray with confidence, and keep themselves from idols.

themes.title: Fellowship with God
themes.body: The letter opens with the aim of fellowship (koinonia), a shared life with the Father, the Son, and one another (1:3). John speaks of it in several ways: knowing God, abiding or remaining in him, being born of him, being his children. This is not a mood but a relationship, and it has visible marks in belief, obedience, and love.

themes.title: The Word made flesh
themes.body: Against teachers who denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, John insists on the physical reality of the incarnation: the life of God was heard, seen, and touched. The cross was a real death in real blood. A Christ who only seemed to be human could not be the atoning sacrifice for sins, and a spirituality that despises the body will soon despise the neighbor.

themes.title: Love as the family likeness
themes.body: God is love, and his love was shown in sending his Son. Those born of God bear the family resemblance. John makes the test concrete: love is laying down one's life and opening one's hand to a brother in need (3:16-18). No one can claim to love the unseen God while hating the brother he can see (4:20).

themes.title: Sin, forgiveness, and holiness
themes.body: John holds together two truths that are easily pulled apart. Believers still sin, and those who deny it deceive themselves, but the blood of Jesus cleanses and God forgives those who confess (1:7-9). At the same time, the one born of God does not settle into a life of sin, because Christ came to take sin away. Grace is neither excuse nor impossible demand.

themes.title: Assurance
themes.body: The letter's closing purpose statement is that believers may know they have eternal life (5:13). Its tests are meant to steady people who had been told they lacked something. Confidence before God rests on his testimony about his Son and on the Spirit he has given, and even when our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts (3:20).

keyChapters.why: The prologue's eyewitness claim, and the teaching that God is light and that those who confess their sins are forgiven and cleansed.
Christ as advocate and atoning sacrifice, the old and new commandment, and the departure of the antichrists.
The Father's love in calling us his children, and love defined by Jesus laying down his life.
Testing the spirits, and the great statement that God is love, shown in the sending of his Son.
Faith that overcomes the world, God's testimony about his Son, and the letter's purpose of assurance.

parts.body:
1 John is short, five chapters, and it can be read aloud in about twenty minutes. It is called a letter, but it has no greeting, no named writer, no named readers and no goodbye. It reads more like a sermon written down by a pastor who knows his people well. He calls them ‘little children’ and ‘beloved’, and he writes because they have been shaken.

Something painful had happened. A group had left their churches. “They went out from us, but they did not belong to us” (2:19). Those who left took with them a new teaching about Jesus. They seem to have denied that the divine Christ had truly come as a man of flesh and blood. And they seem to have said that what a person does with the body, and how he treats his brother, does not touch the spirit. The people who stayed were left wondering. Were the ones who left more spiritual? Had they themselves missed something? Did they really know God at all?

John answers by circling back, again and again, to three marks of people who know God. They believe the truth about Jesus: that he is the Christ, the Son of God, come in the flesh. They keep God's commands and walk as Jesus walked. And they love one another, not only in words but with open hands.

Along the way the letter says some of the most famous things in the Bible about God. “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (1:5). “God is love” (4:8). And it says where that love was seen: “not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (4:10).

Its aim is not to frighten people but to steady them. Near the end John says why he wrote: “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13).

parts.h: Who wrote it: what is known, and what is not
parts.body:
The letter never gives its writer's name. What it does give is a claim. The writer speaks for a group who were there: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands” (1:1). He writes with the authority of an older leader over churches he treats as his own children. That is what the letter itself shows.

The name John comes from the church's memory. From the second century on, Christians named the writer as John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, and the one long held to stand behind the Gospel of John. Irenaeus, a bishop in Lyon writing about AD 180, quotes the letter as John's. The letter's words are very close to the Gospel's: light and darkness, truth and lies, remaining in him, being born of God, the world, the new commandment. Most scholars agree that the Gospel and the three letters come from the same circle, and many think the same hand wrote the Gospel and this letter.

The question is which John. Papias, a bishop in Asia early in the second century, named the apostle John among the Lord's disciples, and then named a second man, ‘the elder John’. His words survive only because the historian Eusebius quoted them in the early 300s. Eusebius read Papias as speaking of two different men. 2 John and 3 John both open with the words “The elder” (2 John 1:1; 3 John 1:1), and some scholars think this elder was a leader of the churches of Asia late in the first century who was not the apostle. Others hold that the apostle himself, by then an old man, simply called himself ‘the elder’, a title that fit him. Still others speak of a circle of churches and teachers shaped by the disciple whom Jesus loved, from which the Gospel and the letters came.

So the honest answer has two parts. What is known: the writer claims to stand among the first witnesses, he led these churches with an old man's authority, and his words are close kin to John's Gospel. What is not known for certain: whether he was John the son of Zebedee, a second John called the elder, or a leader from that circle. These notes do not choose. They call the writer ‘John’, as the church has. The church received the letter early and widely; by about 200 it was read across the churches with the four Gospels and Paul's letters.

parts.h: When, where, and what had gone wrong
parts.body:
The letter gives no date. Most scholars place it late in the first century, around AD 85 to 100, after the Gospel of John or while its way of speaking about Jesus was well known. A smaller number date it earlier, in the 60s. Early tradition places John's last years in Ephesus, the great port city of the Roman province of Asia, on the west coast of what is now Turkey, and most readers think the letter went to churches in that region. The letter itself does not say.

These were house churches, meeting in homes, in a Greek-speaking world full of temples, trade guilds and teachers of every kind. And they had just been through a split. Some had left (2:19). John calls them liars and antichrists, because they deny that Jesus is the Christ (2:22) and will not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (4:2-3).

What exactly did they teach? No one can be sure, and it is wise not to claim more than the letter says. Many scholars see an early form of what the church later called docetism, from the Greek word dokeō, ‘to seem’: the belief that the divine Christ only seemed to have a real body, because a spiritual being could not truly be joined to flesh or die. Irenaeus reports that a teacher named Cerinthus, active in Asia in John's time, taught that the divine Christ came upon the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross. Whether John is answering Cerinthus himself, a group like his, or something less worked out, the shape of the danger is clear. It was a spirituality that looked down on the body, claimed special knowledge, and treated sin and the love of neighbour as things that did not matter.

That helps a reader understand why John writes as he does. He insists on hands that touched Jesus. He insists that the blood of Jesus was real blood. And he insists that knowing God shows in how a person lives and loves.

Do not expect a straight line of argument. John works like a composer with a few themes. He comes back to light, love, truth, obedience and belief, each time from a slightly different angle, and each time a little deeper. A good way to hold it is in five movements.

The Word of life (1:1-4). What the witnesses heard, saw and touched, proclaimed so that the readers may share their fellowship ‘with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ’.

Walking in the light (1:5 to 2:29). God is light. Walking with him means being honest about sin and trusting him to forgive, keeping his commands, loving one's brother, refusing to love the world, and holding to the truth about the Son against the antichrists who have left.

Children of God (3:1-24). The Father's love has made believers his children. His children do not settle into sin, and they love one another as Jesus laid down his life for them.

Testing the spirits; God is love (4:1-21). True spirits confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh. God is love, shown in the sending of his Son, and perfect love drives out fear.

Faith, witness, and knowing (5:1-21). Faith in the Son overcomes the world. God's own witness about his Son gives life. Believers may know they have eternal life, may pray with confidence, and must keep themselves from idols.

Notice the many ‘If we say’ and ‘whoever says’ sentences (1:6, 8, 10; 2:4, 6, 9; 4:20). John keeps testing claims against life.

John keeps giving his readers ways to recognise the truth. “By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments” (2:3). “Whoever loves his brother remains in the light” (2:10). “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God” (4:2). Believing the truth about Jesus, obeying, and loving: the three keep returning, and in chapter 5 John ties them together in one sentence after another.

Two things matter in reading these marks. First, John will not let them be pulled apart. Some people care most about right belief. Some care most about right living. Some care most about love. John says that a person who has one without the others has not understood any of them. Belief in Jesus that never touches the hands is not what John means by belief. Love that does not care who Jesus is has lost its measure, because John learns what love is from the cross (3:16).

Second, the marks were written to steady people, not to make them anxious. The ones who left were claiming a higher knowledge. John tells those who stayed that they are not second-class: “all of you know the truth” (2:20). He is not handing them a checklist to grade themselves on every bad day. He is showing them that the faith they already had was the real thing. The letter's own purpose sentence says so (5:13).

parts.h: Sin, and the one born of God
parts.body:
Readers soon meet the letter's best-known puzzle. In chapter 1 John says, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1:8). Then he gives the remedy: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1:9). But in chapter 3 he says, “No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning” (3:6), and, “Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin, because God’s seed abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God” (3:9). How can both be true?

Christians have read these verses in several ways. Many point to the Greek verbs in chapter 3, which often describe ongoing action. On this reading John means that a child of God does not keep on sinning as a settled way of life, while he still commits sins that need confessing. The BSB's ‘keeps on sinning’ and ‘refuses to practice sin’ follow this reading. Others think the grammar cannot carry all the weight. They read John as speaking of a particular kind of sin: the open, deliberate rejection of God shown by those who left, or sin as ‘lawlessness’ (3:4), a life that refuses God's rule. Others read chapter 3 as describing what the new birth produces in principle and what a Christian is becoming, set against teachers who said sin did not matter. And the Wesleyan tradition has drawn on these verses in teaching that believers can be freed from willful sin. These notes do not choose.

None of these readings teaches that a true Christian never sins. John has already shut that door in chapter 1, and he writes chapter 2 for those who do: “if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One” (2:1). Across the readings the balance is John's own. Do not deny your sin, and do not make peace with it.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: Antichrists, and those who went out
parts.body:
The word ‘antichrist’ appears in the Bible only in the letters of John (2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 1:7). Many readers bring to it a picture of a single figure at the end of the world. It is worth seeing what John himself says.

He says his readers had heard that ‘the antichrist is coming’. Then he says something surprising: “so now many antichrists have appeared. This is how we know it is the last hour” (2:18). He tells them who these are. “Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son” (2:22). In chapter 4 he speaks of ‘the spirit of the antichrist’, which denies Jesus and ‘is already in the world at this time’ (4:3). In John's letters, then, an antichrist is a teacher who denies the truth about Jesus, and the spirit behind such teaching. John's antichrists had been inside the church and had left it.

The prefix ‘anti’ can mean ‘against’ or ‘in place of’. An antichrist opposes Christ, or sets up a false Christ in his place. Elsewhere the New Testament speaks of false Christs (Mark 13:22) and of ‘the man of lawlessness’ (2 Thessalonians 2:3), and many Christians link those passages with John's word. The notes on 2 Thessalonians 2 set out the ways that passage is read.

Over the centuries Christians have often named someone of their own day as the antichrist, or tied the figure to an emperor, a pope, a sultan or a dictator. Such identifications have been made many times. These notes make none. They identify the antichrist of John's letters with no living person, office, church, nation, leader or movement. John's own use points the other way: not to guessing at someone far off, but to testing every teacher by what he confesses about Jesus Christ come in the flesh.

And what of those who left? “They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us” (2:19). Christians read this in line with their wider views. Many Reformed and Calvinist churches read it as a key text for the perseverance of the saints: those who finally fall away show that they never truly belonged. Arminian and Wesleyan Christians hold that a true believer can turn away in unbelief and be lost, and read this verse as describing these particular teachers. Lutheran teaching holds that grace can be lost through unbelief, and points the troubled to Christ in the word and the sacraments. Catholic teaching holds that grace can be lost through grave sin and restored through repentance. These notes do not choose. The doctrine study on perseverance sets the views out more fully.

Twice John writes three words that have been loved ever since: “God is love” (4:8, 16). It matters what he does and does not say. He does not say that love is God, as if every kind of love were divine. He says that God is love, and then he shows what he means: “This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him” (4:9). Love is defined by what God did, not by what we feel.

So love in this letter is concrete. “By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (3:16). The next verse brings it down to a purse and a pantry: “If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him?” (3:17). There was no public welfare in the Roman world, and famine or debt could quickly ruin a family. Love meant opening the hand.

And love casts out a certain kind of fear. “There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment” (4:18). John is not saying that a loving person never feels afraid. He is speaking of the dread of judgment. Those who have come to know God's love in the Son may face the day of judgment with confidence (4:17), because their confidence rests on what God has done.

‘God is love’ does not cancel God's judgment. The same chapter speaks of the day of judgment and of a sacrifice for sins, which shows that sin is serious. Most Christian teaching has held that God's love and his justice are not rivals. Love that did not oppose what destroys the beloved would not be love. The cross shows both: God does not overlook sin, and he bears its cost himself.

The letter is fierce about who Jesus is. He is ‘the Word of life’ whom the witnesses heard, saw and touched (1:1), ‘the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us’ (1:2). He is the Christ, the Son of God, and he came in the flesh (4:2). He is the Righteous One who speaks to the Father for sinners (2:1). He came ‘by water and blood’ (5:6). Many readers think John means that the same Son of God who was baptised also truly died, against teachers who said the divine Christ left before the cross. Others connect the water and blood with the flow from Jesus' side at the cross (John 19:34), or with baptism and the Lord's Supper.

He is “the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world” (2:2). Christians agree that this verse does not teach that everyone will be saved, since the same letter says, “whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life” (5:12). Beyond that they read it differently. Many, including Arminian and much of Lutheran and evangelical thought, read it as teaching that Christ died for every person without exception, a sacrifice offered to all and received by faith. Those who hold to particular or definite atonement, common in Reformed theology, read ‘the whole world’ as people from every nation and not only John's own churches, as John 11:52 speaks of gathering God's scattered children into one. Some hold that Christ's death is enough for all and effective for those who believe. These notes do not choose. All agree that the cross is not the private possession of one group.

The letter's last great sentence says of the Son: “He is the true God and eternal life” (5:20). Grammarians debate whether ‘He’ means the Son or the Father, but many readers, noting that the nearest name is Jesus Christ and that the letter began by calling him ‘the eternal life’, read it as one of the New Testament's clearest confessions that Jesus is God. The church confesses that faith in the Nicene Creed: Jesus Christ is ‘very God of very God’, who ‘came down from heaven’ and ‘was made man’. 1 John is one of the places that confession comes from, and its insistence on a Christ who truly came in the flesh is one of the reasons the church would not let go of either half.

The letter's purpose sentence is near its end: “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). John's Gospel was written so that readers might believe (John 20:31). This letter is written to people who already believe, so that they may know.

Where does that knowing rest? Not first on how strong a person feels. John grounds it in God's own witness: “God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son. Whoever has the Son has life” (5:11-12). He adds the Spirit God has given (3:24; 4:13), and the changed life that shows God's work, in obedience and love. And he speaks tenderly to those whose conscience accuses them: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (3:20).

Christians hold different views of how assurance works. Reformed teaching holds that true believers will persevere and may grow in assurance through God's promises, the Spirit's witness and the fruit of grace, though it may be clouded for a time. Wesleyans stress the Spirit's direct witness that believers are God's children. Lutherans point the troubled to Christ in the preached word and the sacraments. Catholic teaching speaks of firm hope in God's mercy while holding that no one can know with complete certainty, without a special revelation, that he will persevere to the end. All of them read John as writing to give confidence, not fear. These notes do not choose.

If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The first is a matter of the old copies. Older English Bibles, such as the King James Version, read at 5:7-8 that there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost, and that these three are one. The words came into the text through Latin copies and appear in only a handful of late Greek manuscripts, some of them in the margin. Erasmus left them out of his printed Greek New Testament in 1516 and put them into his third edition in 1522, and from there they passed into the King James. The Greek theologians of the fourth-century debates about the Trinity never quoted them, because their Bibles did not have them. Most modern translations leave them out, including those made by scholars who confess the Trinity. The BSB reads simply, “For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood—and these three are in agreement” (5:7-8). Some Christians who hold to the Textus Receptus, the printed Greek text behind the King James, still receive the longer words, resting their case on the Latin tradition and on God's providence over the text the church used. The doctrine of the Trinity never rested on this verse. It was confessed at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 without it. The guide How We Got the New Testament says more.

The second is ‘the sin that leads to death’. “If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he should ask God, who will give life to those who commit this kind of sin. There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin” (5:16). John does not say what he means, and Christians read it in several ways. Some think of sin that God judges with bodily death, as with Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5) or the Corinthians who were sick (1 Corinthians 11:30). Others think of a deliberate, final rejection of Christ, like that of the teachers who left and denied the Son. Some connect it with Jesus' warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The law's line between unintentional sins and sins done ‘defiantly’ (Numbers 15:30) may lie in the background. These notes do not choose.

Three things should be said plainly. John does not tell anyone to stop praying for anyone. His point is the other way: pray for a brother or sister who is caught in sin, and God will give life. Nothing in this verse lets a reader decide that a particular person has committed this sin, or say what any person's state before God is. And nothing in it makes anyone's illness or death a sign of God's judgment; Jesus refused that reasoning (John 9:3).

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

1 John quotes the Old Testament less than almost any book of the New Testament, but it breathes its air. ‘God is light’ echoes the psalm: “The LORD is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 27:1). Confession of sin was part of Israel's worship from the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:21) to the psalms: “I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,’ and You forgave the guilt of my sin” (Psalm 32:5).

The only Old Testament story the letter names is Cain's. “Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother” (3:12). Genesis tells it plainly: “Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him” (Genesis 4:8). John uses Cain to show where hatred leads.

The ‘old commandment’ and the ‘new’ (2:7-8) go back to the law: “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus made it new by its measure: “As I have loved you, so you also must love one another” (John 13:34).

And the letter's picture of people who know God, with his word inside them and their sins forgiven, is the new covenant the prophets promised: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). The ‘anointing’ that teaches believers (2:20, 27) draws on Israel's anointing of kings, priests and prophets. The three witnesses of 5:8 echo the law's rule: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). And the last line, ‘keep yourselves from idols’, is the first commandment in another voice: “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3).

It is not a demand for sinless perfection. John says plainly that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself (1:8), and he writes so that those who sin may know they have an advocate (2:1).

It is not a checklist to make tender consciences anxious. Its marks were written to steady people who had been told they lacked something, so that they might know they have eternal life (5:13).

It is not a licence to call every person you disagree with an antichrist. John uses the word for teachers who denied that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh. It names no one living today, and these notes name no one.

It is not a word that love is only a feeling. Love in this letter is measured by the cross and shown with open hands.

And it is not a book that makes belief unimportant so long as people are kind, or kindness unimportant so long as belief is right. John refuses to separate them.

Read it in one sitting first, aloud if you can. It takes about twenty minutes. Listen for the words that come back again and again: light, love, truth, know, remain, born of God, the world, little children.

Read it with John's Gospel open beside it. Compare the first verses of each (John 1:1-14; 1 John 1:1-4), and compare their purpose sentences (John 20:31; 1 John 5:13).

Remember the split behind it. When John speaks of liars and antichrists, he is speaking of particular teachers who had left. When he speaks of ‘little children’, he is speaking to people who stayed, and he is speaking with love.

Where readers differ, on 3:6-9, on ‘the whole world’, on the sin that leads to death, read more than one view before you settle, and hold your own view as one who may yet be taught.

And let it ask its questions. Do you walk in the light, honest about your sin? Do you love your brother or sister with your hands as well as your words? And where does your confidence before God rest?

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘If we say we have no sin’: honesty about sin, and God's faithful forgiveness.
‘The whole world’: how the churches read the reach of Christ's sacrifice.
‘Many antichrists’: what John means, and why these notes name no one.
‘They went out from us’: those who left, and the readings on perseverance.
‘You do not need anyone to teach you’: the anointing, and the church's teachers.
‘He cannot go on sinning’: beside 1:8-10, the main readings.
‘Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer’.
‘God is greater than our hearts’: a word for the accusing conscience.
‘Test the spirits’: how to tell the Spirit of God from false teaching.
‘God is love’, and the God who judges.
The three witnesses, and the longer words found in later copies.
‘So that you may know’: assurance in 1 John.
‘A sin that leads to death’: the main readings, and what John does not say.
‘He is the true God and eternal life’.

words.line: Greek koinōnia, a shared life: with the Father and the Son, and so with one another (1:3, 7).
God's holiness and truth, with no darkness at all; to walk in it is to live honestly before him (1:5-7).
Greek homologeō, to say the same thing: to agree with God about sin, or about Jesus (1:9; 4:2).
Greek paraklētos, one called alongside to speak for another. Here it is Jesus, before the Father (2:1).
Greek hilasmos, the sacrifice that deals with sin and turns away judgment (2:2; 4:10).
Greek menō, to stay, abide or remain: John's word for a settled, lasting bond with God (2:24, 27-28).
One who opposes Christ or puts a false Christ in his place. In John, teachers who deny the Son (2:18, 22; 4:3).
Greek chrisma. Most read it as the Holy Spirit given to all believers; some, as the gospel they received (2:20, 27).
Greek anomia: sin as refusing God's rightful rule, not only breaking a rule (3:4).
Greek agapē, self-giving love, defined by God sending his Son (4:7-10).
Greek marturia, evidence given to show what is true. God's witness about his Son (5:9-11).
Greek eidōlon, an image of a god, and any false object of worship. The letter's last word (5:21).

timeline.what: The first witnesses hear, see and touch ‘the Word of life’ (1:1-3; John 1:14).
The Romans destroy Jerusalem and its temple.
The date most scholars give for the letter. A smaller number date it in the 60s.
A group leaves the churches, denying that Jesus Christ came in the flesh (2:19; 4:2-3).
Papias names the apostle John and also ‘the elder John’; his words survive in Eusebius.
Irenaeus quotes the letter as John's, and reports the teaching of Cerinthus in Asia.
1 John is received across the churches with the Gospels and Paul's letters.
Eusebius quotes Papias and reads him as naming two men called John.
The councils of Nicaea and Constantinople confess the Trinity.
Words about three witnesses in heaven first appear, in Latin writings, at 5:7-8.
Erasmus prints the Greek New Testament without those words, then adds them in his third edition.

places.name: Ephesus
places.line: The letter names no place. Early tradition places John's last years here, in the Roman province of Asia, and most readers think the churches that saw the split of 2:19 were in this region.

teaching.mapNote: 1 John names no place on earth. It does not say where it was written or where its readers lived. Early tradition places John's last years at Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia, and most readers think the letter went to churches in that region, so the map shows Ephesus alone.
